record.paper_title: SOFT PHYSICS AND INTERMITTENCY : OPEN QUESTION(S) in KRAKOW
record.original_question: In intermittency studies of hadron-induced reactions, do same-sign-particle correlations at very small Lorentz-invariant momentum distance q² reproduce the same effects as analyses in full three-dimensional phase space, and can conventional Bose-Einstein interference between identical particles explain, or at least determine the influence on, the intermittency phenomenon?

evidence.quote: Indeed, the correlation integral method clearly shows that for hadron-induced reactions, same-sign particles contribute mainly at very small q 2 , the Lorentz-invariant momentum distance between near-by particles. Note that a check should be done to know whether this variable gives the same results as the 3− dimensional phase space in terms of rapidity, azimuth and transfer momentum.

Does it mean that the conventional Bose-Einstein interference effect between identical particles can explain the intermittency phenomenon? Or what is the influence of Bose-Einstein correlations on the intermittency problem (as it is asked in ref.[14])?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the phenomenon of intermittency in multiparticle production from hadron–hadron collisions, where one studies the scaling behaviour of normalised factorial moments F_q(δ) of the multiplicity distribution with respect to the size δ of phase-space cells, the empirical fact being that F_q(δ) grows as a power of 1/δ when δ becomes small.

For pairs of same-charge final-state particles, define the Lorentz-invariant squared momentum distance
  q² = −(p₁ − p₂)²,
and consider the correlation integral built from same-sign particle pairs at very small q². Compare this with the analysis performed in the full three-dimensional phase space parametrised by rapidity y, azimuthal angle φ, and transverse momentum p_T.

(a) Do the same-sign-particle correlations at very small q² in hadron-induced reactions reproduce quantitatively the intermittent behaviour observed in the three-dimensional (y, φ, p_T) phase-space analysis?

(b) Can conventional Bose–Einstein interference between identical bosons, modelled e.g. by a two-particle correlation function C₂(q) = 1 + λ exp(−R² q²) (or its analogue), account for the intermittency phenomenon in hadron-induced reactions, and if not, to what extent does it determine or contribute to the observed scaling of factorial moments?
artifact.status_search_result: Subsequent experimental and theoretical work (e.g. NA22 correlation-integral analyses and reviews of intermittency/Bose-Einstein correlations) has established that in hadron-induced reactions same-sign pair correlations dominate the intermittent rise at small q², that correlation integrals show power-law behaviour in Q² consistent with the (y,φ,p_T) analysis, and that Bose-Einstein correlations are a major, though not exclusive, source of the intermittency signal in hadronic collisions. The qualitative answer is therefore largely affirmative, but a fully quantitative decomposition remains a matter of ongoing modelling.

status_evidence.title: Bose-Einstein source of intermittency in hadronic interactions
status_evidence.snippet: Identifies Bose-Einstein correlations as a dominant source of intermittency in hadronic interactions.
status_evidence.claim: BE correlations substantially account for the intermittency signal in hadron reactions.

status_evidence.title: The influence of Bose-Einstein correlations on intermittency in p-pbar collisions at sqrt(s)=630 GeV
status_evidence.snippet: Study of the influence of BE correlations on intermittency in hadron collisions.
status_evidence.claim: Experimental work has quantified the influence of BE correlations on intermittency, supporting them as a primary contributor.

status_evidence.title: New NA22 Results on Correlations
status_evidence.snippet: Correlation integrals exhibit power law dependence on Q²; BE ratio rises steeply as Q²→0 compatible with a power law.
status_evidence.claim: Q²-based correlation integral analysis reproduces intermittent power-law behaviour seen in 3D phase space.
